title: Autism and neurodiversity
blurb: Support autistic people with and without a learning disability using NICE guidance on assessment, interventions to avoid and sensory adjustments.
question: Kai, 19, is autistic and has a moderate learning disability. In a busy emergency department he is screaming and hitting his head, and his notes say he has had abdominal pain since yesterday. A staff member says 'that's just his autism'. What should the nurse do first?

teach.h: Autism: a different way of experiencing the world
teach.body: Autism is a lifelong developmental difference in social communication and interaction, with repetitive behaviours, strong interests and preferences for routine, and often sensory differences such as sensitivity to noise, light or touch. Neurodiversity means this is part of natural human variation, not a fault to fix. Autistic people can have any level of intellectual ability: some also have a learning disability, many do not.

Dates
teach.caption: The 2021 update changed wording to 'autistic people'; it did not change the recommendations.

children.label: Consider AQ-10
children.sub: Score 6+ or clinical suspicion: full assessment

children.label: Brief assessment
children.sub: Ask about social interaction, routines, sensory needs

teach.caption: CG142 1.2.3-1.2.4. Diagnosis is clinical: do not routinely use biological tests, genetic tests or neuroimaging (1.2.11).

teach.h: Core features of autism: what NICE says
teach.caption: Adults: CG142 1.4.13-1.4.15 (anticonvulsants, chelation, exclusion diets and supplements) and 1.4.21-1.4.22 (antipsychotics; antidepressants not routinely). Children and young people: CG170 1.3.2.

teach.body: For behaviour that challenges, NICE advises psychosocial interventions first. An antipsychotic may be considered with a psychosocial intervention when response has been limited, or alone if the behaviour is so severe that psychosocial work cannot be delivered. A specialist prescribes, considering a low starting dose, reviews the effects at 3 to 4 weeks and stops the medicine if there is no clinically important response at 6 weeks. Anticonvulsants are not routinely used for behaviour that challenges. Oliver McGowan, an autistic young man, died in 2016 after an antipsychotic he and his family had asked not to be given.

steps.label: Before
steps.sub: Visual supports, photos, what will happen

steps.label: Arrive
steps.sub: First or last appointment; quiet space

steps.label: During
steps.sub: Low light and noise, personal space, explain before touch

steps.label: After
steps.sub: Record what worked for next time

teach.caption: Under 19s, CG170 1.1.9-1.1.10: visual supports, personal space, lighting, noise and wall colours; appointments at the start or end of the day. Adults, CG142 1.1.8: personal space, visual supports, colours, lighting and noise.

teach.body: Noise, light, crowds, waiting and unexpected touch can overwhelm an autistic person. Distress may look like shouting, running, self-injury or shutting down. It is not deliberate. Reduce the input (quieter space, fewer people, one person talking), give time and predictable information, and use the person's own communication methods. Always ask whether pain or illness lies behind new distress.

review of benefit after starting an antipsychotic for behaviour

teach.h: Scenario: Kai in the emergency department
teach.body: Head-hitting with a day of abdominal pain may be how Kai is communicating pain, made worse by a noisy department. The nurse moves him to a quiet room, lowers the lights, keeps one familiar person talking, and asks his carer about his usual signs of pain and his communication methods. A prompt clinical assessment for the cause of his pain follows. Saying 'that's just his autism' is diagnostic overshadowing.

teach.text: Autism is not a learning disability, and medicines do not treat the core features of autism. Language: many autistic people prefer 'autistic person' to 'person with autism'. Ask the person and record their preference.

items: Autism: social communication, routines and interests, sensory differences; any intellectual level.
Adults: AQ-10 (score 6+) without moderate or severe LD; brief assessment with it; no routine scans or genetic tests.
Not for core features: antipsychotics, antidepressants, anticonvulsants, exclusion diets, chelation.
Behaviour that challenges: psychosocial first; antipsychotic by a specialist, review at 3–4 weeks.
Adjust: visual supports, quiet space, light and noise, first or last appointment.

summary: You can now describe autism as a neurodevelopmental difference that may or may not occur with a learning disability, apply NICE guidance on assessment and on interventions not to use, and make sensory and environmental adjustments while watching for pain and illness behind distress.

A.q: Which NICE guideline covers the recognition, referral and diagnosis of autism in children and young people under 19?
options: CG170
CG142
CG128
NG11
A.why: CG128 covers recognition, referral and diagnosis in under 19s; CG170 covers their support and management; CG142 covers adults.

whyNot.0: CG170 covers support and management in under 19s, not diagnosis.
whyNot.3: NG11 covers behaviour that challenges in people with learning disabilities.

A.q: Ayaan, 8, is autistic and needs a blood test. His mother says new places frighten him. Which preparation is most in line with NICE CG170?
options: A surprise approach so he has less time to worry
Visual supports showing each step, and a quiet space
Holding him firmly so that the test is over quickly
Waiting in the main area so he gets used to the noise
A.why: CG170 1.1.9-1.1.10 recommends visual supports and adjusting the environment (noise, lighting, personal space) for autistic children and young people.

whyNot.0: Unpredictability increases distress for many autistic children.
whyNot.2: Restraint is a last resort, not a planned preparation.
whyNot.3: Exposure to a noisy waiting area increases sensory overload.

A.q: The family of Jade, 26, who is autistic, ask about chelation therapy they have read about online to 'treat her autism'. What does NICE CG142 advise?
options: Chelation can help if her blood metal levels are raised
Chelation should be tried before any psychosocial support
Chelation can be used if a specialist prescribes it
Chelation should not be used for autism in adults
A.why: NICE CG142 (1.4.13-1.4.15) advises against chelation, anticonvulsants and exclusion diets for the core features of autism in adults.

whyNot.0: Chelation is not a treatment for autism.
whyNot.1: Psychosocial interventions are recommended; chelation is not.
whyNot.2: Specialist prescribing does not make chelation a recommended autism treatment.

B.q: Sam, 30, is autistic and has a severe learning disability. His behaviour that challenges is so severe that a psychosocial intervention cannot be delivered. According to NICE CG142, what may be considered?
options: An anticonvulsant to stabilise his mood and behaviour
An antipsychotic alone, with benefit reviewed at 3 to 4 weeks
An antipsychotic started by his GP and reviewed at 6 months
No medication until psychosocial work has run for 6 months
B.why: CG142 1.5.8: an antipsychotic may be considered alone when psychosocial intervention cannot be delivered because of the severity of the behaviour, prescribed by a specialist with review at 3 to 4 weeks.

whyNot.0: Anticonvulsants are not routinely used for behaviour that challenges (1.5.9).
whyNot.2: Prescribing should be by a specialist, with early review at 3 to 4 weeks.
whyNot.3: CG142 allows an antipsychotic when severity prevents psychosocial work.

B.q: A GP suggests an anticonvulsant to reduce aggression in Callum, 28, who is autistic and does not have epilepsy. What does NICE CG142 advise?
options: Anticonvulsants are first-line for aggression in autism
Anticonvulsants are not routinely used for this behaviour
Anticonvulsants are suitable if an antipsychotic is refused
Anticonvulsants are suitable once he has a learning disability
B.why: CG142 1.5.9: do not routinely use anticonvulsants for the management of behaviour that challenges in adults with autism.

whyNot.0: Psychosocial interventions come first; anticonvulsants are not routine.
whyNot.2: Refusing an antipsychotic does not make anticonvulsants appropriate.
whyNot.3: A learning disability does not change this advice.

B.q: A nurse is writing an admission summary for a new patient who is autistic and does not know how they prefer autism to be described. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Use 'suffers from autism' as the clinical term
Use 'high-functioning' to describe their abilities
Ask how they describe themselves and use that
Use the wording in the GP letter without asking
B.why: Respecting how a person describes their identity is person-centred practice (NMC Code 1, 2). Many autistic people prefer identity-first language; NICE's 2021 update uses 'autistic people'.

whyNot.0: 'Suffers from' frames autism as a disease and is widely considered disrespectful.
whyNot.1: Functioning labels can hide real support needs and are often disliked.
whyNot.3: The GP letter may not reflect the person's own preference.

C.q: Kai, 19, is autistic with a moderate learning disability. In a busy emergency department he is screaming and hitting his head; he has had abdominal pain since yesterday. A colleague says 'that's just his autism'. What should the nurse do first?
options: Request sedation so that he can be examined safely
Move him to a quiet room and assess for a cause of pain
Ask security to hold him to prevent a head injury
Record it as his autism and wait for his carer to arrive
C.why: Distress may be communicating pain, made worse by sensory overload. Reducing sensory input and promptly assessing for a cause avoids diagnostic overshadowing and restrictive practice.

whyNot.0: Sedation is restrictive and not a first step; it also masks his signs.
whyNot.2: Physical restraint is a last resort and can worsen distress.
whyNot.3: Attributing distress to autism is diagnostic overshadowing and delays assessment.

C.q: Tom, 40, has a mild learning disability. His support worker thinks he may be autistic. Which first step is most in line with NICE CG142?
options: Use a brief assessment, as he has a learning disability
Arrange an MRI scan and genetic tests to look for autism
Consider the AQ-10 and offer full assessment if he scores 6+
Offer a trial of risperidone while he waits to be assessed
C.why: CG142 1.2.3: for adults without a moderate or severe learning disability (Tom's is mild), consider the AQ-10; a score of 6 or more, or clinical suspicion, leads to comprehensive assessment.

whyNot.0: The brief assessment (1.2.4) is for adults with a moderate or severe learning disability.
whyNot.1: Scans and genetic tests are not used routinely to diagnose autism (1.2.11).
whyNot.3: Antipsychotics do not treat core features and are not a diagnostic step.

C.q: Mr Lewis, 35, is autistic and on a surgical ward. He is distressed by the bright lights and alarms in his bay and is refusing his observations. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Document the refusal and inform the doctor on call
Ask his relatives to persuade him to accept the checks
Move him nearer the nurses' station so he is safer
Reduce light and noise, explain each step and agree timings
C.why: His refusal is driven by sensory overload. Adjusting the environment and making observations predictable (Equality Act s20; CG142) is the practicable first step.

whyNot.0: Documenting without adjusting leaves the barrier in place.
whyNot.1: Persuasion by relatives does not address the cause of his distress.
whyNot.2: Areas near the nurses' station are usually busier and noisier.

reteach.title: Change the room, not the person
reteach.question: An autistic person is distressed in a clinic. What should change first: the person, or the environment?

blocks.body: Most distress in clinical settings comes from noise, light, waiting, crowds and unpredictability. Changing these is a reasonable adjustment and often all that is needed. Medicines do not treat the core features of autism; they may be considered for behaviour that challenges by a specialist, usually alongside psychosocial support.

blocks.text: Autistic does not mean learning disabled. Ask the person how they communicate and what helps.

explain.body: Autism is a difference in social communication, routines and sensory processing. It occurs at any intellectual level; some autistic people also have a learning disability.

test.q: Which statement about autism and learning disability is accurate?
options: Autism is a form of mild learning disability
Every autistic person has a learning disability
They are separate conditions that can co-occur
A learning disability is a form of autism
test.why: Autism and learning disability are distinct; some people have both.

whyNot.0: Autism is not a form of learning disability.
whyNot.1: Many autistic people do not have a learning disability.
whyNot.3: A learning disability is not a form of autism.

explain.body: No moderate or severe LD: AQ-10, 6 or above (or clinical suspicion) means comprehensive assessment. Moderate or severe LD: brief assessment. No routine biological, genetic or imaging tests.

test.q: Pauline, 50, has a severe learning disability. Her carers notice she covers her ears in busy places, insists on the same route every day and rarely seeks others out. Her GP asks how to begin assessing for autism. Which approach does NICE CG142 recommend?
options: Consider a brief assessment instead of the AQ-10
Use the AQ-10 with her carers answering for her
Arrange neuroimaging to confirm the diagnosis
Wait for a crisis before considering assessment
test.why: CG142 1.2.4: for adults with a moderate or severe learning disability, consider a brief assessment of possible autism.

whyNot.1: The AQ-10 is for adults without a moderate or severe learning disability.
whyNot.2: Neuroimaging is not used routinely for diagnosis.
whyNot.3: Assessment should be considered when autism is suspected.

explain.body: For core features: no antipsychotics, antidepressants or anticonvulsants, no exclusion diets, supplements or chelation. Use psychosocial interventions and adjustments.

test.q: Ruby, 10, is autistic. Her father asks the school nurse for a tablet to help her join in with other children and play less repetitively. What does NICE CG170 advise?
options: An antidepressant may reduce her repetitive play
An antipsychotic is first-line for social difficulties
Medicines are not recommended for core features
A casein-free diet should be tried before medicines
test.why: CG170 1.3.2: do not use antipsychotics, antidepressants, anticonvulsants or exclusion diets for the core features of autism in children and young people.

whyNot.0: Antidepressants are not recommended for core features.
whyNot.1: Antipsychotics are not recommended for core features.
whyNot.3: Exclusion diets are not recommended either.

explain.body: Visual supports, personal space, attention to lighting, noise and wall colours, and the first or last appointment of the day to reduce waiting (CG170 1.1.9-1.1.10).

test.q: Leon, 14, is autistic and finds crowds and waiting very distressing. He is due an eye test at a busy hospital eye clinic. Which adjustment reflects NICE CG170?
options: A mid-morning slot when most staff are free
The first or last appointment and a quiet place
A longer appointment in the main waiting area
A group visit with other children to reduce fear
test.why: CG170 advises attention to noise and personal space, and appointments at the start or end of the day to minimise waiting.

whyNot.0: Mid-morning is often the busiest time.
whyNot.2: The main waiting area increases sensory load.
whyNot.3: Group settings increase social and sensory demand.
